ada_sensing · exposure simulation · validation run

ParamISP simulates the ImageNet-ES-Diverse exposure grid from a single auto-exposure shot

Pipeline: AE sRGB → inverse ISP (ParamISP, CVPR 2024, official pre-trained weights) → pseudo-RAW, scaled by the physical exposure ratio t·ISO/N² → forward ISP conditioned on the target parameters → simulated sRGB. Scored against the dataset's real captures of the same 27 configs (3 apertures × 3 shutters × 3 ISOs), 10 samples × 6 lighting environments = 1,620 comparisons.

Error decomposition & post-hoc calibration

Fitting corrections on 400 random sim/real pairs decomposes the error: a global brightness gain recovers +3.6 dB, a per-channel color gain a further +1.3 dB, and the rest is structural — the cross-camera ISP gap (consistent with the ≈27.5 dB identity-round-trip ceiling). Note the headline PSNR is flattered by near-black cells (58% of the grid); well-exposed configs sit at ≈19 dB raw.

A per-environment post-hoc correction (3×3 linear color matrix + monotonic tone LUT, black point pinned, fit only on the 5 calibration images) was applied to all eval sims:

Caveat the numbers hide: the least-squares fit earns its PSNR partly by desaturating (middle row above is visibly grayer than both raw sim and real). Global corrections are at their ceiling; the remaining gap is config-dependent and spatially varying — a network-level fix (per-camera fine-tuning), not a LUT-level one. Calibrated sims saved as simcal_param_*.jpg alongside the raw ones.

The physical simulator wins

A weight-free alternative run on the identical benchmark: linearize → scale by t·ISO/N² → clip → re-encode, where the per-channel tone curve is a 33-knot monotone LUT fitted to this camera from the same 5 calibration images (3 alternating iterations of curve fit and per-env AE-exposure refinement; median-based, which avoids the least-squares desaturation above). v1 assumes the standard sRGB curve; v2 uses the fitted one.

The fitted physical model beats the pretrained network in every band, numerically and visually (no desaturation, no warm cast — middle row vs top row above). Reading: on planar scenes the exposure problem is a tone curve plus a scalar; what ParamISP adds — a learned ISP of other cameras — costs more than it contributes cross-camera, while the physical model spends its calibration budget directly on the only unknown that matters. Still missing from both: ISO noise synthesis and any spatially varying ISP behaviour. Physical sims saved as phys_param_*.jpg; the fitted curve at results/phys_tonecurve.npy; code in run_phys_es.py (+ the standalone module es_sim.py with a fittable shot/read-noise model).

Calibration & honest caveats

AE exposure estimation. The AE JPEGs carry no EXIF, so the AE exposure product E = t·ISO/N² was estimated per environment: initialized from per-pixel linear-luminance ratios vs well-exposed reference captures, then refined through the simulator by brightness matching — using 5 calibration images kept separate from the 10 evaluated samples. One scalar per environment; no other ground truth enters the simulation.
  • Cross-camera: the ES-Diverse capture camera is not among ParamISP's training cameras; the run uses the multi-camera pre-training weights with neutral WB/CCM chosen by round-trip self-consistency (identity round-trip ≈27.5 dB). Residual tone/color mismatch is visible in the grids — sims trend slightly darker and warmer than real at some settings.
  • No noise module: unlike the original Neural Camera Simulators, ParamISP has no explicit noise injection; real ISO 16000 grain is not reproduced.
  • Aperture is photometric only: valid here because ES-Studio photographs planar prints. On real 3D scenes (video), f-number changes depth of field — this pipeline will not simulate that.
  • Overexposure artifacts: heavily blown configs (1/4s at high ISO) show orange/magenta casts in simulation where the real capture clips to clean white.
